catalog_quote: No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz de la palabra. Cuando dos raíces se juntan para formar una palabra compuesta, la segunda raíz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las sílabas se añaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales actúan como si fueran el segundo tema de un compuesto; en otras palabras, reciben el acento principal. En los siguientes ejemplos, la sílaba acentuada se indica con letras mayúsculas: ... SIna• sabio ... xbanYID tlacuache ... new_statements.quote: No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz de la palabra. Cuando dos raíces se juntan para formar una palabra compuesta, la segunda raíz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las sílabas se añaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales actúan como si fueran el segundo tema de un compuesto; en otras palabras, reciben el acento principal. [...] Los préstamos mantienen la sílaba acentuada del español, aunque puede ser que se les quite una o más sílabas.
new_statements.translation: Stress is not written in Zapotec. In general, Zapotec stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root of the word. When two roots join to form a compound word, the second root receives the main stress. When syllables are added by prefixes or pronominal suffixes, the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the root. However, many adverbial suffixes act as if they were the second stem of a compound; in other words, they receive the main stress. [...] Loanwords keep the stressed syllable of Spanish, although one or more syllables may be dropped.
new_statements.citation: Long C., Rebecca & Sofronio Cruz M. 2000 [1999]. Diccionario zapoteco de San Bartolomé Zoogocho, Oaxaca. 2a ed. electrónica. Vocabularios indígenas 38. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (text layer of the held PDF, Long & Cruz 2000 [1999], SIL Vocabularios 38, 2a ed. electronica, fetched sources from Wayback copy of sil.org/mexico). At txt lines 22658-22684 (printed p. 407, 'Gramatica Zapoteca' sec. 0.4 'El acento') the quoted passage is present word for word: 'No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penultima silaba de la raiz de la palabra. Cuando dos raices se juntan... la segunda raiz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las silabas se anaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penultima silaba de la raiz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales... reciben el acento principal.' followed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is root-bound: it falls on the penultimate syllable of the root (on the root itself when monosyllabic); aspect/plural prefixes and pronominal enclitics never shift it, so its position in the surface word varies (CHAGW-be', ches-AGW-be', cheseBE'). In compounds and with many adverbial suffixes the second root/suffix takes main stress (xbanYID, chagw-ŽAT). Spanish loans keep Spanish stress. Independently confirmed by Sonnenschein 2004 §2.5 p. 34: 'Stress in Zoogocho Zapotec primarily falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem, except... where a word is composed of more than one root (incorporated noun or adverb) in which case the accent falls on the second root.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Long & Cruz speak of 'acento principal' on the second root of compounds, implying the first root keeps a lesser stress, but no explicit secondary-stress rule is given; Sonnenschein says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and many adverbial suffixes take main stress on the second element; Spanish loans retain Spanish stress (camIS 'camisa', regLADW 'arreglado'); occasional orthographic ambiguities from affixation (CHEbe' 'él traga' vs cheBE' 'se sienta de nuevo'). Minor discrepancy: Sonnenschein (p. 35) says adverbial suffixes do not affect stress placement, while Long & Cruz say many adverbial suffixes attract main stress (though Sonnenschein p. 34 also puts accent on an incorporated adverb root).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/stem, not the orthographic/phonological word: prefixes and pronominal enclitics are outside the stress domain; clitics have no independent stress (Sonnenschein §2.6). The language is also tonal (Long & Cruz: 4 levels + 7 glides; Sonnenschein: 3 levels + rising + falling), with stress described separately from tone. Statements concern word-level (citation-form) stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the Zapotec of San Bartolomé Zoogocho, Villa Alta district, Sierra Norte de Oaxaca (zpq, zoog1238); Long & Cruz note the dictionary also reflects the closely similar speech of Yalina, Tabehua and Zoochina/Zoochila neighbours only incidentally. No dialect mismatch.

sources.note: Gramática zapoteca §0.4 'El acento' (p. 407): stress not written; falls on the penultimate syllable of the root; in compounds the second root takes main stress; prefixes and pronominal suffixes do not move it (stays on root penult); many adverbial suffixes behave like a second compound stem and take main stress; Spanish loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable; examples with stressed syllable in caps (SIna', CHAGW-be', ches-AGW-be', chagw-ŽAT, camIS). §0.5 (pp. 407-408): tonal language, 4 level tones + 7 glides, analysis preliminary.
